slides: Let's continue with plugging in numbers, and how to choose the number.

slides.say: How do we choose the number? First, we check every restriction in the question. The number must obey all of them. If it says x is at least four, x can't be two.
at: If it says x is at least four

slides.say: If a must be positive and whole, it can't be zero, and it can't be one half. And if a letter is in the bottom of a fraction, it can't be zero, because we can't divide by zero.
at: If a must be positive and whole
in the bottom of a fraction

slides.say: In a figure, choose values that fit the given conditions. Don't choose an angle just because it looks that size in the drawing. The figure may not be drawn to scale.
And a good first try is often the edge of what's allowed. If x is at least four, try four itself.

Second, we choose an easy number that's allowed. Zero is often the fastest, because every term with zero in it becomes zero. Zero is out only when it breaks a restriction, like the bottom of a fraction.
Here's an example. x times the bracket x plus one. The choices are x squared plus x, three x, x squared plus one, and four x.
Is there a restriction? No, x can be any number. So zero is allowed, and we take x equals zero. Zero times one is zero. So the right choice must give zero when x is zero.
Third, we check what zero rules out. Choice number one says x squared plus x. Zero plus zero is zero, so it stays. Choice number two says three x. Three times zero is zero, so it stays too.
Choice number three says x squared plus one. Zero plus one is one, not zero, so it's out. Choice number four says four x. Four times zero is zero, so it stays.

Three choices give zero, so zero can't tell them apart. That's why we don't stop at the first choice that fits. Fourth, we try another easy allowed number, and we check only the three choices that are left.
Now x equals one. One times two is two, so the right choice must give two. x squared plus x is one plus one, two, so it stays. Three x is three, and four x is four. They aren't two, so they're out.
at: x squared plus x is one plus one

slides.say: Only x squared plus x is left, so it's the answer. No third try is needed. So that's how we choose. Check the restrictions, choose an easy allowed number, and see what it rules out. Try another number only if more than one choice is left.
at: Only x squared plus x is left

slides.say: Here's an example where zero isn't allowed. x squared times x to the power of three, all divided by x. The choices are x to the power of four, x to the power of five, x to the power of six, and x to the power of three.
First the restrictions. x is at the bottom of the fraction, and we can't divide by zero. So zero isn't allowed here.
The next easy number is one. One to any power is one. So the question gives one, and all four choices give one too. Nothing is ruled out, so we need another try.
Now x equals two. Two squared is four, and two to the power of three is eight. Four times eight is thirty-two, and thirty-two over two is sixteen. So the right choice must give sixteen.
The choices give sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four and eight. Only x to the power of four gives sixteen. So this one try rules out the other three.

So zero and one are fine to start with. But with powers in the choices, they often make every choice give the same result. Then we just take the next easy allowed number. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
